title: Secure Computation Meets Distributed Universal Optimality
abstract: We present a new algorithmic approach to distributed secure algorithms that is based on combining two independent lines of research: \emph{secure computation} and \emph{distributed universal optimality}. Our end result provides round-efficient distributed algorithms that protect the privacy of the graph vertices against a (possibly large) coalition of semi-honest adversaries. \textbf{Secure Computation:} The notion of perfect privacy dates back to Yao [FOCS '82], and has been extensively addressed by the Cryptographic community over the years. Most of the prior work considers the Multi-Party-Communication (MPC) model, in which the parties are fully connected. Considerably less is known on the (round) complexity of secure algorithms for general graphs, especially under the classical message passing models, such as the \congest\ model. For any biconnected $D$-diameter graph, a recent line of works [Parter and Yogev, SODA 19, ICALP 19, PODC 19] presented a simulation result that protects against a \emph{single} semi-honest corruption, by paying an overhead of $D \cdot \poly(\Delta)$ \congest\ rounds, where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree. Due to an inherent structural barrier, the generalization of the current framework to handling $f$ corruptions, \emph{provably} leads to an overhead of $O(\Delta D)^{\Theta(f)}$ rounds. This can also be shown to be tight for the class of store-and-forward algorithms\footnote{In which nodes can only propagate messages as atomic units, without the ability to mix multiple messages together.}. \textbf{Secure Computation \& Universal Optimality.} We present an improved framework for secure computation which bypasses the current exponential in $f$ barrier. For every graph $G=(V,E)$ with vertex-connectivity $\widetilde{\Omega}(f)$, our simulation provides a round overhead of $\poly(\Delta)\cdot \widehat{O}(\shortcut{G})$.\footnote{The notation $\widehat{O}(\cdot)$ hides $2^{O(\sqrt{\log n})}$ factors.} The graph measure $\shortcut{G}$ (Shortcut Quality) captures the universal optimal complexity of many network optimization tasks in the (non-secure) \congest\ model, as demonstrated in a recent breakthrough result of [Haeupler, Wajc and Zuzic, STOC 2021]. We are hopeful that the extended graph-theoretic machinery provided in this paper will find further applications in secure computation and beyond.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Motivation. Modern distributed networks are insecure by
nature, and the private information of their users is under a
constant threat of leakage to untrusted parties. While earlier
Cryptography was concerned with two users, Alice and Bob,
who want to communicate privately, today, Alice and Bob are
part of the internet [Quote taken from Goldwasser’s keynote
talk of PODC’97 [1]]. The modern instantiations of private
communication are captured by an arbitrary network of n
users who want to perform computations among themselves,
while keeping their local data secret. Examples include online
elections, electronic bidding, joint data-base computation and
blockchains. The security of these computations introduces
a joint cryptographic and graph-theoretical challenge. The
cryptographic aspect has been formulated by the Multi-Party
Computation (MPC) setting which aims at securely solving a
joint function of n users that are fully connected by a complete
graph. MPC provides a clean and convenient abstraction for
secure computation, as explained by Goldreich in his introduction to this model:
[Goldreich, [2]] For simplicity we consider a model
in which each pair of parties is connected by a
reliable and private (or secret) channel. The issues
involved in providing such channels are beyond the
scope of this exposition.
The focus of this paper is precisely the graph theoretical challenge that arises when one needs to establish these channels
(i.e., paths with certain desired properties) in the given communication network, which might have an arbitrary structure.
In the most general form of the setting, given is a collection of
{(si , ti )} pairs where each si wishes to exchange messages mi
with ti in a secure manner, i.e., revealing no information on mi
to a semi-honest adversary controlling a subset of F ∗ nodes in
the graph. The graph nodes have no information on the identity
of F ∗ . Dolev, Dwork, Waarts and Yung [3] fully characterized

In particular, we aim at understanding the graph-theoretic

As we discuss soon, the existing secure algorithms require

Ideally, we would like to provide efﬁcient secure algorithms

Distributed (Non-Secure) Computation for Any Network.
The area of distributed graph algorithms (DGA) lies on the
other extreme of this security vs. network generality tradeoff.
The main focus of DGA is in understanding the graph structure
of each given network and utilize it for providing efﬁcient
distributed solutions that meet the communication bottlenecks
of the network. This most often comes at the cost of sacriﬁcing
the privacy of the users. Indeed, existing distributed algorithms
are highly insecure, as throughout their executions the nodes
gain information on the input and output of their neighbors
and beyond.
We use a standard message passing model of distributed
computing called CONGEST [11], where the network is
abstracted as an n-vertex graph G = (V, E), with one
processor on each network node. Initially, these processors do
not know the graph. They solve the given graph problems via
communicating with their neighbors. Communications happen
in synchronous rounds, where per-round, each processor can
send one O(log n)-bit message to each of its neighboring
processors. Since the inﬂuential paper of Garay, Kutten, and
Peleg [12], the DGA area has devoted a concentrated effort
to network optimization problems such as minimum-spanning
trees, shortest-paths, minimum-cut computation, etc. Recent
years focused on universal optimal algorithms that perform
(nearly) as fast as possible for every given graph. Ghaffari and
Haeupler [13] introduced the seminal “low-congestion short
cuts” framework for designing algorithms that run in O(SQ
(G)) rounds. Informally, the parameter SQ(G) characterizes
the number of rounds required to route single bit messages
between {(si , ti )} pairs connected by vertex-disjoint paths in
G, where the pairs can be chosen in an adversarial manner.

Graphical Private Channels. We consider the graph-theoretic
formulation of a private channel, which roughly speaking
consists of a collection of G-paths, such that at least one of

Secure Simulation of a Single Round. To illustrate our ideas
we focus on the simpliﬁed setting of compiling a single-round
algorithm A into an equivalent f -secure algorithm A . For
example, A might be the non-secure algorithm for identifying
the vertex of largest value in each neighborhood (Q. 1). This
already captures most of the techniques. Assume that in Alg.
A, each vertex u holds an O(log n)-bit (private) value xu . It is
then required for each vertex u to compute some joint function
gu of the values of its neighbors N + (u). The f -security
property requires that the semi-honest adversary controlling
the F ∗ nodes learns nothing on the input and output values of
the reliable nodes, in the information-theoretic sense, except
for what can be determined from the input and output of the
F ∗ nodes. Prior work [28] provided 1-secure solutions by
simulating the Private-Simultaneous-Messages (PSM) protocol
of [38]. While there are extensions of the PSM protocol to
handle a coalition of f corruptions, their message complexity
might be exponential12 in f , see e.g., [8], [39].
Our approach is based on simulating the BGW protocol
[6] (see Theorem IV.2) over each neighborhood N + (u) to
securely compute gu , for all nodes u, simultaneously. The
output of the BGW protocol is guaranteed to be held jointly
by all parties, N + (u), in the form of secret shares. Thus in
the last round, each u can learn its own output (by getting the
shares from its neighbors) and “nothing” more than that. As
the BGW protocol is designed for complete networks, the key
challenge is in implementing private channels between each
reliable pair x, y ∈ N + (u) (denoted as 2-hop neighbors), for
every u ∈ V . Overall we need to communicate safely and
simultaneously between all 2-hop neighbors, hence O(Δ2 n)
pairs13 . The running time should be sublinear in the number
of pairs, and the length of the private channel paths. Our
compiler then has two steps. The ﬁrst step computes the private
channels between all 2-hop neighbors. Since this step does not
depend on the private inputs of the nodes, the computation
of the channels can be done in a non-secure manner. In the
distributed output, each vertex knows its neighbors on each of
the channels to which it belongs, along with the channel-ID.
In the second step, we simulate the non-secure algorithm A by
emulating the BGW protocol over each N + (u), where each
BGW-message between x, y ∈ N (u) will be sent securely
over the x-y private-channel, as we formally introduce next.
